patient.name: Tariq Mahmood
patient.complaint: Eight months of low back and buttock pain, worst first thing in the morning
background: Software developer in Stratford; plays five-a-side football
Father has 'a stiff back' and walks stooped
Has taken ibuprofen on and off from the pharmacy

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a young man whose back pain is worse in the morning and better with exercise, often plus one 'A' clue (red eye, heel pain, early diastolic murmur). Also 'most likely finding on examination' (reduced lateral lumbar flexion, Schober's <5 cm).

points: Tariq, 26, has **8 months** of low back and buttock pain.
Stiff for **over an hour** every morning.
Pain **eases with football**, worse sitting at his desk.
Wakes him in the **second half of the night**.

steps.q: Which feature of Tariq's pain most strongly suggests an inflammatory rather than mechanical cause?
o: Pain worse at the end of the day
steps.r: Inflammatory back pain **improves with exercise and worsens with rest**. Mechanical pain is the opposite; radiation below the knee suggests a radiculopathy.

steps.lead: A young man with chronic inflammatory back pain: think of a disease that fuses the **spine and sacroiliac joints**.
Tariq is **male, under 40**, and his stooped father hints at a **family history** and possibly **HLA-B27**.

visual.title: Morning stiffness
visual.label: Tariq 75 min
visual.caption: Morning stiffness **over 30 minutes** is the inflammatory cut-off. Mechanical back pain stiffens briefly, if at all.

points: **Tender left Achilles** insertion; he limps first thing.
Side-bending to slide his hand down his leg is **reduced**.
Chest expansion is reduced at **3 cm**.

steps.lead: Tariq has the classic pattern: **morning stiffness, better with exercise, night pain, fatigue, Achilles enthesitis** and **reduced lateral flexion**, the early sign.

steps.title: Is this inflammatory back pain?
nodes: Better with exercise, worse with rest
Think axial spondyloarthritis: refer to rheumatology
steps.caption: Several of these together in a young adult should push you away from 'mechanical back pain'.

steps.lead: Ask Tariq about the **'A's**: red painful eyes, heel pain, palpitations and breathlessness all point to extra-articular AS.
Untreated, Tariq risks the path his father took: **bamboo spine**, a stooped posture and **osteoporotic fractures**.

steps.text: A **stooped 'question mark' posture** and **bamboo spine** are **late** findings. A young patient in an SBA usually has a normal posture; the early clue is **reduced lateral lumbar flexion**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (pelvic X-ray of the sacroiliac joints) versus 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (MRI of the sacroiliac joints), and Schober's test as the bedside measure.

steps.lead: At the bedside, Tariq's lumbar flexion is measured with **Schober's test**.

visual.title: Schober's test: increase on forward flexion
visual.label: Tariq 3.5 cm
visual.caption: Marks 10 cm above and 5 cm below the dimples of Venus. They should separate by at least **5 cm** on bending forward.

steps.title: Tariq's bloods
steps.text: Raised inflammatory markers and a **negative rheumatoid factor**: a **seronegative** picture. HLA-B27 supports, but does not prove, the diagnosis.

steps.q: Which imaging should be requested first for Tariq?
o: Pelvic X-ray of the sacroiliac joints
steps.r: The **pelvic X-ray of the SI joints** is the initial investigation. MRI is the gold standard if the X-ray is normal or early disease is suspected.

steps.lead: Tariq's X-ray shows **bilateral sacroiliitis** with subchondral sclerosis: the finding needed for the modified classification criteria.
Had Tariq's X-ray been normal, **MRI of the SI joints** would show bone marrow oedema of early sacroiliitis long before X-ray changes appear.

steps.title: Initial vs gold standard
head: Test
Role
Shows
rows: Sacroiliitis, sclerosis, erosions; may be normal early

steps.lead: Ultrasound can grade Tariq's **Achilles enthesitis**, and he joins **2-yearly osteoporosis screening**.

steps.text: Lead-in decides the answer: **'initial'** = pelvic X-ray of the SI joints; **'diagnostic' / 'gold standard'** = **MRI of the SI joints**.
**HLA-B27** is not diagnostic: most HLA-B27 positive people never get AS. It is a risk marker, never the 'most appropriate diagnostic investigation'.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (NSAID plus physiotherapy), 'next step' after NSAID failure (TNF-alpha inhibitor), and the AS patient with a painful red eye who needs same-day ophthalmology.

steps.q: Tariq has confirmed AS. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
steps.r: **NSAIDs plus exercise/physiotherapy** are first-line. Methotrexate helps peripheral joints, not the axial spine; steroids are not a long-term answer.

steps.lead: Tariq starts **naproxen** and a structured **physiotherapy** and stretching programme; he keeps up the football.

points: Three months later: still stiff for an hour each morning.
He has tried **two NSAIDs** at full dose.
CRP remains raised; he is missing work.

steps.lead: NSAIDs have failed, so Tariq moves to a **TNF-alpha inhibitor**; secukinumab is kept for if TNF inhibitors are unsuitable.

visual.title: Tariq's response to treatment
visual.caption: Little change on NSAIDs; stiffness and CRP fall once the **TNF-alpha inhibitor** starts.

steps.title: Treatment ladder in AS
steps.caption: Screen for TB before any biologic.

points: A year on, Tariq calls: **left eye painful, red, blurred**.

steps.q: What should Tariq's GP do now?
steps.r: A painful red eye with blurred vision in AS is **anterior uveitis** until proven otherwise: **same-day ophthalmology**.

steps.lead: Tariq has **anterior uveitis**: he is seen the same day and given **cyclopentolate** to relax the ciliary muscle.
These guide Tariq's long-term care: **2-yearly osteoporosis screening** and the **modified New York criteria** used to classify his AS.

steps.text: Do not give **chloramphenicol** for a red eye in AS. Painful, photophobic and blurred is **uveitis**, not conjunctivitis, and needs ophthalmology the same day.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanism questions: why HLA-B27 matters, why AS inflames entheses rather than synovium, why the spine fuses, and the cytokine targeted by a named biologic.

steps.lead: Tariq is **seronegative** (no rheumatoid factor) and **HLA-B27 positive**: the classic spondyloarthropathy profile.
Tariq's **Achilles pain** and **reduced chest expansion** are both enthesitis: at the heel and at the costochondral joints.
Without control of inflammation, Tariq's **syndesmophytes** would bridge his vertebrae, as his father's have.

steps.r: Adalimumab is an anti-**TNF-alpha** monoclonal antibody. TNF-alpha and IL-17 are the key cytokines driving AS inflammation.

steps.lead: Tariq's uveitis shares the **IL-17/IL-23 axis** with AS; the same pathway links psoriasis and IBD.

visual.title: Chest X-ray in long-standing AS (his father)
visual.caption: **Apical fibrosis** is one of the 'A's of AS: upper zone fibrosis, unlike the lower zone pattern of IPF.

steps.text: The 'A's are extra-articular: lung apex, eye, aortic valve, Achilles, AV node.
AS is **enthesitis-first**, rheumatoid arthritis is **synovitis-first**. That is why AS gives heel pain and fusion, while RA gives symmetrical small-joint erosions.

mcq.q: Which genetic marker is most strongly associated with ankylosing spondylitis?
mcq.r: **HLA-B27**. HLA-DR4 is rheumatoid arthritis; DQ2 is coeliac disease.

mcq.q: Which is an early examination sign of ankylosing spondylitis?
mcq.r: **Reduced lateral lumbar flexion** is early; stooped posture and bamboo spine are late.

mcq.q: Which eye complication is classically associated with AS?
mcq.r: **Anterior uveitis** (iritis): painful red eye, blurred vision, photophobia; hypopyon if severe.

mcq.q: Which valve lesion is one of the 'A's of AS?
mcq.r: **Aortic regurgitation**, heard as an early diastolic murmur.

mcq.q: What Schober's test result suggests AS?
mcq.r: The marks should separate by at least 5 cm; **under 5 cm** suggests reduced lumbar flexion.

mcq.q: What is the gold standard investigation for AS?
mcq.r: **MRI of the SI joints** is far more sensitive than X-ray, especially in early disease.

mcq.q: What is first-line management of AS?
What is the second-line treatment if NSAIDs fail in AS?
mcq.r: **TNF-alpha inhibitor** (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab); secukinumab if TNF inhibitors are unsuitable.

mcq.q: What is the primary site of inflammation in AS?
mcq.r: AS is an **enthesitis**, not primarily a synovitis.

mcq.q: What are the bony outgrowths that bridge vertebrae in AS called?
mcq.r: **Syndesmophytes** bridge vertebral bodies to form the bamboo spine.

prompts.q: What is ankylosing spondylitis and who gets it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem is nearly always a young man; the HLA type is a favourite one-liner.

points.p: Chronic inflammatory disease fusing the spine and sacroiliac joints
points.why: It is axial first; peripheral joints are less prominent.
Classic SBA patient: a man in his 20s.
New inflammatory back pain over 40 makes AS less likely.
A stooped relative is a common stem hint.

prompts.q: Describe the classic back pain of AS.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: these features separate inflammatory from mechanical back pain.

points.why: Mechanical pain is worse with activity.

prompts.q: What are the examination findings in AS, early and late?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'most likely finding on examination' wants the early sign in a young patient.

points.p: Reduced forward flexion: Schober's under 5 cm
points.why: Less than 5 cm increase is abnormal.
Ankle or heel pain in a young man with back pain.
Late; unlikely in a 25 year old stem.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one 'A' in a stem (red eye, murmur, heel pain) is often the hook.

prompts.q: What are the eye features and the long-term complications of AS?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: a painful red eye with blurred vision in AS is uveitis; sudden back pain after minor trauma is a fracture.

points.p: Iritis: eye pain, blurred vision, redness
points.why: Photophobia too; distinguishes it from conjunctivitis.
A rigid spine breaks with little force.

prompts.q: What are the initial and gold standard investigations for AS, and what do they show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the lead-in word ('initial' or 'diagnostic') picks the answer.

points.p: Initial: pelvic X-ray of the sacroiliac joints
points.why: May be normal in early disease.

points.p: Sacroiliitis: most specific finding, needed for classification criteria
points.why: Modified New York criteria need radiographic sacroiliitis.

points.p: Squaring of vertebrae, syndesmophytes, erosions and sclerosis, bamboo spine
Gold standard: MRI of the sacroiliac joints
points.why: Much more sensitive than X-ray for early disease.

prompts.q: What other tests are used in AS: bedside, second-line and long-term?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: know the Schober's cut-off and the 2-yearly osteoporosis screen.

points.p: Schober's test: increase under 5 cm suggests AS
Ultrasound second-line for inflammation and enthesitis

prompts.q: Outline the treatment ladder for AS.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'initial management' = NSAID plus exercise; 'next step' after NSAID failure = TNF-alpha inhibitor.

points.why: Two NSAIDs are usually tried before biologics.

points.p: If TNF inhibitors unsuitable: IL-17 inhibitor (secukinumab)

prompts.q: How do you manage an acute red painful eye in a patient with AS?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: urgency is the answer, not antibiotics.

points.why: Not conjunctivitis: it is painful with blurred vision.
Routine optician review is the distractor.

points.p: Topical cyclopentolate for severe uveitis or hypopyon
points.why: Relaxes the ciliary muscle and prevents adhesions.

prompts.q: Why does AS cause enthesitis, a bamboo spine and links with uveitis, psoriasis and IBD?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: entheses not synovium; TNF-alpha and IL-17 explain the biologics.

points.p: HLA-B27 presents self-peptides/misfolded proteins, triggering inflammation at entheses
Erosion then new bone (syndesmophytes) bridging vertebrae
Shared IL-17/IL-23 axis with uveitis, psoriasis and IBD
TNF-alpha and IL-17 drive the cascade: targets for biologics
points.why: Adalimumab blocks TNF; secukinumab blocks IL-17A.

glossary.Ankylosing spondylitis: Chronic inflammatory arthritis of the spine and sacroiliac joints that can fuse them over years.
glossary.HLA-B27: A class I HLA gene variant strongly linked to ankylosing spondylitis and other seronegative spondyloarthropathies.
glossary.Sacroiliac joint: Joint between the sacrum and the iliac bone of the pelvis; inflamed early in AS.
glossary.Sacroiliitis: Inflammation of the sacroiliac joints, the most specific X-ray finding in AS.
glossary.Enthesis: The point where a tendon or ligament attaches to bone.
glossary.Enthesitis: Inflammation where tendons or ligaments insert into bone, such as the Achilles insertion.
glossary.Spondyloarthropathy: Family of HLA-B27 linked arthritides affecting the spine and entheses: AS, psoriatic, reactive and enteropathic arthritis.
glossary.Seronegative: Rheumatoid factor negative; used for the spondyloarthropathies.
glossary.Schober's test: Bedside test of lumbar forward flexion; marks should separate by at least 5 cm.
glossary.Lateral lumbar flexion: Side-bending of the lower spine; reduced early in AS.
glossary.Syndesmophytes: Vertical bony bridges growing from vertebral body margins in AS.
glossary.Bamboo spine: Late X-ray appearance of a fused spine bridged by syndesmophytes.
glossary.Squaring: Loss of the normal concave front of vertebral bodies from inflammation at the corners.
glossary.Subchondral sclerosis: Increased bone density just beneath the joint surface, seen on X-ray.
glossary.Anterior uveitis: Inflammation of the iris and ciliary body causing a painful red eye, photophobia and blurred vision.
glossary.Hypopyon: A layer of pus (white cells) in the anterior chamber of the eye.
glossary.Cyclopentolate: Anticholinergic eye drop that dilates the pupil and relaxes the ciliary muscle, easing uveitis pain.
glossary.Aortic regurgitation: Leaky aortic valve; causes an early diastolic murmur.
glossary.Apical fibrosis: Scarring of the upper zones of the lungs, an extra-articular feature of AS.
glossary.AV node block: Delayed or blocked conduction from atria to ventricles, seen on ECG as heart block.
glossary.First-degree heart block: PR interval longer than 200 ms with every P wave conducted.
glossary.Amyloidosis: Deposition of abnormal protein (AA amyloid in chronic inflammation) in organs such as the kidney.
glossary.Costochondritis: Inflammation where ribs join the sternum; reduces chest expansion in AS.
glossary.Plantar fasciitis: Inflammation of the plantar fascia insertion at the heel, causing heel pain.
glossary.NSAIDs: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs that inhibit COX enzymes, e.g. ibuprofen and naproxen.
glossary.TNF-alpha: Pro-inflammatory cytokine central to AS and RA inflammation.
glossary.TNF-alpha inhibitor: Biologic that blocks TNF-alpha, e.g. adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab.
glossary.Etanercept: Fusion protein that binds and neutralises TNF-alpha.
glossary.Infliximab: Chimeric monoclonal antibody against TNF-alpha, given by infusion.
glossary.Secukinumab: Monoclonal antibody against IL-17A, used when TNF inhibitors are unsuitable.
glossary.IL-23: Cytokine that sustains IL-17 producing T cells; the IL-17/IL-23 axis.
glossary.Modified New York criteria: Classification criteria for AS requiring radiographic sacroiliitis plus clinical features.
glossary.DXA: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry; the scan that measures bone density for osteoporosis.
glossary.Osteoporosis: Low bone mass and weak bone structure raising fracture risk.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein, a blood marker of inflammation.
glossary.ESR: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate, a non-specific marker of inflammation.
glossary.Rheumatoid factor: Autoantibody against IgG Fc, positive in many with RA and negative in spondyloarthropathies.
glossary.Dimples of Venus: Skin dimples over the posterior superior iliac spines, the landmark for Schober's test.

technique.stem: A 24 year old man has a 9 month history of low back pain. He is stiff for over an hour every morning and the pain improves when he goes to the gym. The pain wakes him in the early hours. He also has pain at the back of his right heel. Neurological examination of the legs is normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about back pain: decide **inflammatory vs mechanical** first.

clues: stiff for over an hour every morning
improves when he goes to the gym
wakes him in the early hours
pain at the back of his right heel
steps.x: Young man, chronic, morning stiffness over 30 min, better with exercise, night pain, plus **Achilles enthesitis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Inflammatory back pain with enthesitis in a young man: **ankylosing spondylitis**.

elim: Disc prolapse is sudden, often after lifting, with sciatica below the knee.
Spinal stenosis affects older people and causes leg pain on walking eased by bending.
Mechanical pain worsens with exercise and does not cause long morning stiffness.
Spondylolisthesis gives mechanical pain, worse on extension, without enthesitis.

steps.x: **B. Ankylosing spondylitis.** Rule: young + morning stiffness over 30 min + better with exercise = inflammatory back pain.

technique.stem: A 27 year old man has 5 months of inflammatory low back pain and buttock pain. He is HLA-B27 positive and his CRP is raised. A pelvic X-ray of the sacroiliac joints is reported as normal. His rheumatologist still suspects early ankylosing spondylitis.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: 'Diagnostic', not 'initial': the X-ray is done, so they want the **gold standard**.

clues: pelvic X-ray of the sacroiliac joints is reported as normal
steps.x: Early disease with a normal X-ray: X-ray changes lag behind inflammation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **MRI of the SI joints** detects early sacroiliitis (bone marrow oedema).

elim: CT shows bony change but misses early inflammation and gives radiation.
DXA screens for osteoporosis, not sacroiliitis.
Ultrasound assesses peripheral joints and enthesitis, not deep SI joint inflammation.
Lumbar X-ray changes (squaring, syndesmophytes) appear later still.

steps.x: **C. MRI of the sacroiliac joints.** Rule: normal X-ray but suspicion persists = MRI SIJ.

technique.stem: A 34 year old man with ankylosing spondylitis has persistent back pain and morning stiffness despite two different NSAIDs at full dose and a physiotherapy programme. A TNF-alpha inhibitor was started but stopped because he developed demyelinating symptoms, so TNF inhibitors are now considered unsuitable.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

steps.x: 'Next step': place him on the treatment ladder.

clues: TNF inhibitors are now considered unsuitable
steps.x: NSAIDs failed and anti-TNF is ruled out: the next rung is the IL-17 inhibitor.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IL-17 inhibitor: secukinumab.**

elim: Adalimumab is a TNF-alpha inhibitor, now unsuitable.
Etanercept is a TNF-alpha inhibitor, now unsuitable.
Infliximab is a TNF-alpha inhibitor, now unsuitable.
Long-term oral steroids do not control axial AS and worsen osteoporosis.

steps.x: **E. Secukinumab.** Ladder: NSAID + physio → TNF-alpha inhibitor → IL-17 inhibitor.

technique.stem: A 29 year old woman with ankylosing spondylitis is started on adalimumab after NSAIDs failed to control her symptoms. Her morning stiffness and CRP improve over three months.
technique.q: Which is the mechanism of action of adalimumab?

steps.x: A drug mechanism question: name the target of adalimumab.
Second-line after NSAIDs in AS is the **TNF-alpha inhibitor** class; adalimumab is one.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Anti-**TNF-alpha** monoclonal antibody.

elim: IL-6 receptor blockade is tocilizumab.
IL-17A blockade is secukinumab.
CD20 depletion is rituximab.
COX inhibition is how NSAIDs work.

steps.x: **E. Neutralises TNF-alpha.** '-mab' drugs in AS: adalimumab/infliximab = TNF, secukinumab = IL-17.

practice.stem: A 23 year old man has a 7 month history of low back and alternating buttock pain. He is stiff for about an hour each morning and feels better after cycling to work. Sitting at his desk makes it worse. He feels constantly tired. His father had a 'fused spine'. Straight leg raise is negative bilaterally.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Young man with inflammatory back pain, buttock pain, fatigue and a family history: ankylosing spondylitis. Mechanical pain would worsen with exercise.

steps.x: Diagnosis: inflammatory or mechanical back pain?

clues: stiff for about an hour each morning
steps.x: Classic inflammatory features plus **family history** and **fatigue**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Ankylosing spondylitis.**

elim: Disc prolapse gives sciatica and a positive straight leg raise.
Mechanical pain worsens with activity and stiffness is brief.
Psoriatic arthritis needs psoriasis or nail changes.
Reactive arthritis follows an infection and is usually acute.

steps.x: **A. Ankylosing spondylitis.** Better with exercise, worse at rest = inflammatory.

practice.stem: A 25 year old man has 6 months of low back pain and morning stiffness lasting 45 minutes that eases with exercise. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. He has full power and normal reflexes in both legs.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his spine?
practice.e: Reduced lateral lumbar flexion is the early examination sign of AS. Straight leg raise, reflex loss and saddle anaesthesia are nerve root or cauda equina signs.

steps.x: An examination finding question: the stem describes AS, so pick its **early** sign.
Inflammatory back pain, neurology normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Early AS sign: **reduced lateral lumbar flexion** (and Schober's under 5 cm).

elim: AS flattens lordosis; it does not increase it.
Straight leg raise is positive in disc prolapse.
Reflexes are normal in the stem.
Saddle anaesthesia is cauda equina syndrome.

steps.x: **D. Reduced lateral lumbar flexion.** Early = lateral flexion; late = stooped posture.

practice.stem: A 31 year old man with ankylosing spondylitis has a 1 day history of a painful red right eye with blurred vision and pain in bright light. The redness is most marked around the cornea. The right pupil is small. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Painful red eye with photophobia, blurred vision, perilimbal redness and a small pupil in AS is anterior uveitis. Angle-closure gives a fixed mid-dilated pupil.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a red eye in a patient with AS.
Photophobia, ciliary flush and a small pupil = iritis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Anterior uveitis**, the commonest extra-articular 'A' of AS.

elim: Angle-closure gives a fixed, mid-dilated pupil, haloes and vomiting.
Conjunctivitis is gritty with discharge and normal vision.
Episcleritis is mildly uncomfortable with normal vision.
Subconjunctival haemorrhage is painless with normal vision.

steps.x: **B. Anterior uveitis.** AS + painful red eye + photophobia = same-day ophthalmology.

practice.stem: A 62 year old man with ankylosing spondylitis for 35 years has increasing breathlessness on exertion. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and collapsing in character, and BP 158/48 mmHg. There is an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge, loudest with him sitting forward in expiration. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: Resting ECG
visual.caption: PR interval prolonged at 240 ms: first-degree heart block.

practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his murmur?
practice.e: Early diastolic murmur, collapsing pulse and wide pulse pressure in long-standing AS = aortic regurgitation. The first-degree block is the 'AV node block' A.

steps.x: Name the valve lesion from the murmur.

clues: early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge
steps.x: Wide pulse pressure and early diastolic murmur, with AV conduction disease on ECG.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Aortic regurgitation**, an 'A' of AS.

elim: Aortic stenosis is ejection systolic with a slow-rising pulse.
Mitral regurgitation is pansystolic at the apex.
Mitral stenosis is mid-diastolic at the apex.
Tricuspid regurgitation is pansystolic with giant v waves.

steps.x: **A. Aortic regurgitation.** AS 'A's on the heart: aortic regurgitation and AV node block.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man with long-standing ankylosing spondylitis has sudden severe mid-back pain after slipping on a step. He has a fixed stooped posture. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg. Leg neurology is normal. A previous DXA scan was abnormal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A rigid, osteoporotic AS spine fractures with minor trauma. Normal calcium and ALP and no fever make metastases and discitis unlikely.

steps.x: Diagnosis of acute back pain in a patient with known AS.
Late AS (fused, stooped) plus osteoporosis plus minor trauma.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Osteoporotic (fragility) vertebral fracture**, a recognised AS complication.

elim: Cauda equina needs saddle anaesthesia or sphincter problems; neurology is normal.
Discitis gives fever and a much higher CRP.
Metastases suggest weight loss, raised calcium or ALP.
Spinal stenosis causes gradual claudication-type leg pain.

steps.x: **D. Osteoporotic vertebral fracture.** AS raises fracture risk through fusion and osteoporosis.

practice.stem: A 21 year old man has 10 months of pain at the back of both heels and low back stiffness each morning that improves with running. He has no diarrhoea, urinary symptoms or rash and no recent illness. Both Achilles insertions are tender. Schober's test shows a 3 cm increase.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Chronic inflammatory back pain, bilateral Achilles enthesitis, Schober's under 5 cm and seronegative bloods = AS. No preceding infection rules out reactive arthritis.

steps.x: Diagnosis: heel pain plus back stiffness in a young man.

clues: no diarrhoea, urinary symptoms or rash
Schober's test shows a 3 cm increase
steps.x: Enthesitis, inflammatory back pain, reduced lumbar flexion, no trigger infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Ankylosing spondylitis.**

elim: Rupture is sudden, unilateral and does not cause back stiffness.
Gout is acute monoarthritis; urate is normal.
Reactive arthritis follows GI or GU infection, which is excluded.
RA is a symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis; RF is negative.

steps.x: **B. Ankylosing spondylitis.** Enthesitis + inflammatory back pain + Schober's under 5 cm.

practice.stem: A 26 year old man has 8 months of low back pain with morning stiffness lasting over an hour. The pain improves with exercise and his chest expansion is reduced. His GP suspects ankylosing spondylitis and refers him to rheumatology. No imaging has yet been done.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: Pelvic X-ray of the sacroiliac joints is the initial investigation in AS. MRI is the gold standard if the X-ray is normal.

steps.x: 'Initial' investigation, not 'diagnostic'.

clues: No imaging has yet been done
steps.x: Imaging starts with the cheap, available test.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pelvic X-ray of the sacroiliac joints**, looking for sacroiliitis.

elim: CT adds radiation and is not first-line.
HLA-B27 supports but cannot diagnose AS.
MRI is the gold standard, used if the X-ray is inconclusive.
RF is for RA and is negative in AS.

steps.x: **E. X-ray of the sacroiliac joints.** Initial = X-ray; diagnostic = MRI.

practice.stem: A 30 year old man has 4 months of inflammatory buttock and low back pain. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 120/74 mmHg. Pelvic X-ray of the sacroiliac joints is normal. The rheumatologist still suspects early ankylosing spondylitis.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: MRI of the SI joints is the gold standard and detects early sacroiliitis when the X-ray is still normal.

steps.x: 'Diagnostic' after a normal X-ray: gold standard.

clues: Pelvic X-ray of the sacroiliac joints is normal
steps.x: Short history: X-ray changes have not appeared yet.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **MRI of the SI joints.**

elim: Bone scans are non-specific and not used to diagnose AS.
CT misses early inflammation and adds radiation.
DXA measures bone density for osteoporosis screening.
Ultrasound assesses enthesitis, not deep SI joint inflammation.

steps.x: **D. MRI of the sacroiliac joints.**

practice.stem: A 24 year old man is diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis after a pelvic X-ray shows bilateral sacroiliitis. He has morning stiffness for an hour and night pain. He has no history of peptic ulcer, asthma or kidney disease and has not taken any regular treatment.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: First-line AS treatment is an NSAID plus physiotherapy/exercise. Biologics come only after NSAIDs fail.

steps.x: 'Initial' management of newly diagnosed AS.

clues: no history of peptic ulcer, asthma or kidney disease
has not taken any regular treatment
steps.x: No contraindication to NSAIDs and treatment-naive.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **NSAID (ibuprofen or naproxen) + physiotherapy/exercise.**

elim: Adalimumab is second-line after NSAID failure.
Methotrexate does not help axial AS.
Oral steroids are not used long term in axial AS.
Secukinumab is for when TNF inhibitors are unsuitable.

steps.x: **B. Ibuprofen and an exercise programme.** Never skip the physio half.

practice.stem: A 29 year old man with ankylosing spondylitis has ongoing back pain and morning stiffness despite 3 months of two different NSAIDs at full dose and regular physiotherapy. Screening for tuberculosis is negative and he has no contraindication to biologics.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: After NSAID failure, the next step is a TNF-alpha inhibitor such as adalimumab. Secukinumab is reserved for when TNF inhibitors are unsuitable.

steps.x: 'Next step': NSAIDs have already failed.

clues: despite 3 months of two different NSAIDs
steps.x: NSAID failure, safe to start a biologic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **TNF-alpha inhibitor**: adalimumab.

elim: Hydroxychloroquine is a DMARD for RA and lupus, not AS.
Steroid injections give short relief only.
Methotrexate does not treat axial AS.
Secukinumab comes if TNF inhibitors are unsuitable; here they are fine.

steps.x: **A. Adalimumab.** NSAID fail → anti-TNF → IL-17 inhibitor.

practice.stem: A 33 year old woman with ankylosing spondylitis phones her GP with a 1 day history of a painful red left eye, blurred vision and discomfort in bright light. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. Visual acuity is reduced in the left eye.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: A painful red eye with reduced vision in AS suggests anterior uveitis, which needs same-day ophthalmology. A routine referral risks synechiae and vision loss.

steps.x: Initial management: how urgently and where?
Painful, photophobic, reduced vision: **anterior uveitis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent same-day ophthalmology assessment.**

elim: Aciclovir is for herpetic eye disease; no dendritic ulcer or rash is described.
Routine referral is too slow for uveitis.
Chloramphenicol treats bacterial conjunctivitis.
Cromoglicate treats allergic conjunctivitis.

steps.x: **C. Same-day ophthalmology assessment.** Then cyclopentolate if severe.

practice.stem: A 27 year old man with ankylosing spondylitis has reduced chest expansion of 2 cm and pain over his anterior chest wall where the ribs meet the sternum. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. His chest X-ray is normal and spirometry shows no airway obstruction.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his reduced chest expansion?
practice.e: AS is an enthesitis: inflammation at costochondral (and costovertebral) insertions stiffens the rib cage. The normal chest X-ray excludes apical fibrosis and effusion.

steps.x: A mechanism question explaining a sign of AS.

clues: where the ribs meet the sternum
steps.x: Chest wall pain at rib insertions with normal lungs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Enthesitis** at the costochondral joints (costochondritis).

elim: Apical fibrosis would show on the chest X-ray.
AS does not cause muscle weakness of the chest wall.
An effusion would be seen on the chest X-ray.
AS is enthesitis-first, not synovitis-first.

steps.x: **B. Enthesitis at the costochondral joints.** Enthesitis explains Achilles pain, plantar fasciitis and costochondritis.
